title: 07. Google ADK: Day 14 — ADK Web UI, A2A Protocol & MCP Server Mode
summary: Run agents locally with a browser UI, expose them over HTTP, and connect agents across services
objectives: Why Web UI, A2A, and MCP Matter

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Run agents locally with a browser UI, expose them over HTTP, and connect agents across services

Day 14 / 15
ADK v2.7.0 (Aug 2026)
Python 3.10+

🎯 Learning Objectives

- Start `adk web` and navigate the Web UI (chat, sessions, state inspector, Visual Builder)

- Drive agents programmatically via the REST API (`/run`, `/run_sse`, sessions)

- Expose an agent over the A2A protocol with `to_a2a()` and consume it with `RemoteA2aAgent`

- Serve ADK tools as an MCP server consumable by Claude Desktop / Cursor / any MCP client

- Understand which features are dev-only vs production-ready

sections.title: 1. Why Web UI, A2A, and MCP Matter
sections.body:
Building an agent in a Jupyter cell is the easy part. The hard part is **operating** it: debugging a multi-turn conversation, inspecting session state mid-flight, sharing an agent with a teammate who doesn't want to install Python, or wiring two agents built by different teams into one workflow. ADK's Web UI, REST API, A2A protocol, and MCP server mode are the four tools that bridge the gap between "it works in my notebook" and "it's a service my team can use".

The **Web UI** is your dev cockpit — `adk web` boots a FastAPI server on port 8000 with a chat interface, a session browser, a state inspector, and (new in 2.0) a Visual Builder drag-and-drop workflow editor. It is the fastest way to test a new agent, share a demo URL with a PM, or replay a failing conversation. Behind the same FastAPI app sits a fully documented **REST API** — `/list-apps`, `/run`, `/run_sse`, sessions CRUD — that lets any HTTP client (curl, a React frontend, a Slack bot) drive your agents programmatically.

Once you have multiple agents, **A2A (Agent2Agent)** lets them talk across services. Wrap one agent with `to_a2a(root_agent, port=8001)` and it auto-publishes a JSON "agent card" at `/.well-known/agent-card.json`. Another ADK service consumes it via `RemoteA2aAgent(name="dice", agent_card="http://localhost:8001/.../agent-card.json")`. This is how cross-team, cross-language, and cross-cloud agent networks are built. Finally, **MCP server mode** flips the usual "ADK consumes MCP tools" pattern: your ADK tools become MCP tools that Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP-aware client can call. By the end of today, you'll have run an agent through the Web UI, scripted it via curl, exposed it over A2A, and served its tools as MCP.

💡 Key Concept

ADK's surface area is **three protocols on one FastAPI app**: the Web UI (browser chat), the REST API (HTTP/JSON for programs), and the A2A endpoint (HTTP/JSON-RPC for other agents). All three call into the same `Runner`, so they're interchangeable — what you build for the Web UI works unchanged behind curl, and curl-driven flows work unchanged when consumed by another ADK agent over A2A.

sections.title: 2. Core Concepts
sections.body:
### 2.1 `adk web` — the Dev Cockpit

`adk web` starts a FastAPI server with a built-in browser UI on port 8000 (default). It's the **development mode** for ADK — point it at a folder of agent packages and you get a chat interface, session browser, state inspector, event timeline, and (in Python only) the Visual Builder workflow editor.

```bash
# Basic usage
adk web                                  # serves ./agents on :8000

# Common options
adk web --port 3000 --host 0.0.0.0       # custom port and host
adk web --with_ui                         # explicitly enable UI (default true)
adk web --no-reload                       # disable auto-reload (Windows/MCP)
adk web --session_service_uri="sqlite:///sessions.db"
adk web --artifact_service_uri="gs://my-bucket/artifacts/"
adk web --memory_service_uri="rag://my-corpus-id"
adk web --a2a                             # expose A2A endpoint too
adk web --trace_to_cloud --otel_to_cloud  # observability
```

The full options list (v2.6.0/v2.7.0): `--port` (8000), `--host` (`127.0.0.1`), `--session_service_uri`, `--artifact_service_uri`, `--memory_service_uri`, `--reload`/`--no-reload` (default `true`), `--with_ui`, `--a2a`, `--trace_to_cloud`, `--otel_to_cloud`, `--url_prefix`, `--trigger_sources`, `--enable_features`, `--disable_features`, `--eval_storage_uri`, `--extra_plugins`, `--log_level`.

⚠️ Important

**ADK Web is for development only — never production.** There's no auth, no rate limiting, no TLS, and the auto-reload mode restarts the server on every file change (great for dev, fatal for prod). For production, use `adk deploy cloud_run`, `adk deploy agent_engine`, or a custom FastAPI app via `get_fast_api_app()` — all covered in Day 15.

### 2.2 The Web UI Features

When you open `http://localhost:8000` in a browser, you get four panels:

1. **Chat** — send messages to any agent in the `agents/` folder. Supports streaming (token-by-token), tool-call inspection (expand each function call), and full event timeline.
2. **Sessions** — list all sessions across users, switch between them, replay a session, or delete. Critical for debugging "the agent worked yesterday, broke today" — diff yesterday's session state vs today's.
3. **State Inspector** — view the full `session.state` dict including `user:` and `app:` prefixed keys. You can even edit state in-place to test "what if the user's preferred language were French?".
4. **Visual Builder (Python only)** — drag-and-drop workflow editor. Drop an LlmAgent node, connect it to a tool node, configure instruction in a side panel, and export to `agent.py`. Includes an AI assistant that suggests node configurations.

The state inspector alone is worth the price of admission — it's the difference between guessing what's in `state["user:preferred_lang"]` and seeing it live, mutating it, and watching the next turn reflect your change.

### 2.3 The REST API — Five Endpoints You Need

The same FastAPI app behind the Web UI exposes a clean REST surface. All endpoints are on port 8000 (or whatever `--port` you set):

| Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/list-apps` | List available agent apps (folder names) |
| `POST` | `/apps/{app_name}/users/{user_id}/sessions/{session_id}` | Create session (body = initial state dict) |
| `GET` | `/apps/{app_name}/users/{user_id}/sessions/{session_id}` | Get session (state + events) |
| `PATCH`/`DELETE` | `/apps/{app_name}/users/{user_id}/sessions/{session_id}` | Update / delete session |
| `POST` | `/run` | Run agent — collects all events, returns as a JSON list |
| `POST` | `/run_sse` | Run agent — streams events via Server-Sent Events (token-level with `streaming: true`) |

The `/run` body shape:

```json
{
  "appName": "my_sample_agent",
  "userId": "u_123",
  "sessionId": "s_123",
  "newMessage": {"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "Hello"}]}
}
```

Use `/run` for batch jobs and `/run_sse` for interactive UXs where you want to render tokens as they arrive. `run_sse` supports a `streaming: true` flag inside `newMessage` to enable token-level streaming (otherwise it streams at the event level — tool calls, function responses, final text).

🚀 Pro Tip

The `/run_sse` endpoint is what powers the Web UI's chat. If you're building your own frontend (React, Vue, mobile), `/run_sse` is the endpoint to use — it gives you the same UX as the Web UI without the UI. Each SSE event is a JSON-serialized `Event` object with `content`, `actions`, `author`, and `partial` fields.

### 2.4 A2A Protocol — `to_a2a()` and `RemoteA2aAgent`

A2A (Agent2Agent) is an open protocol for agents to discover and invoke each other across services. ADK implements it via `to_a2a()` (expose) and `RemoteA2aAgent` (consume). Install with the `[a2a]` extra:

```bash
pip install google-adk[a2a]
```

**Exposing an agent** is a one-liner:

```python
from google.adk.a2a.utils.agent_to_a2a import to_a2a

a2a_app = to_a2a(root_agent, port=8001)
# Then: uvicorn my_agent.agent:a2a_app --host localhost --port 8001
```

`to_a2a()` parameters: `agent` (required), `host` (default `"localhost"`), `protocol` (default `"http"`), `port` (default `8000`), `push_config_store`, `agent_card`, `runner`. Internally it creates an `A2aAgentExecutor`, `InMemoryTaskStore`, `InMemoryPushNotificationConfigStore`, `DefaultRequestHandler`, and a Starlette app. If you don't pass `agent_card`, it's auto-generated from your agent's `name`, `description`, and tools — and served at the well-known path `/.well-known/agent-card.json`.

**Consuming an agent** is just as easy:

```python
from google.adk.agents.remote_a2a_agent import RemoteA2aAgent, AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH

dice_agent = RemoteA2aAgent(
    name="dice_roller",
    description="Rolls dice and returns the result.",
    agent_card=f"http://localhost:8001/a2a/dice_agent{AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH}",
    # use_legacy=False,  # opt into new ADK-A2A extension
    # config=A2aRemoteAgentConfig(
    #     a2a_message_converter=...,
    #     request_interceptors=[...],
    # ),
)

root_agent = Agent(
    name="coordinator",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    sub_agents=[dice_agent],
)
```

The default `use_legacy=True` keeps backward compatibility with the original A2A spec; set `use_legacy=False` to opt into ADK's extended A2A features (richer artifact passing, long-running task tracking, reasoning trace preservation).

```
                   A2A (Agent2Agent) PROTOCOL FLOW
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                          │
│   ┌──────────────────────┐                  ┌──────────────────────┐    │
│   │  Service A (port 8001)│                  │  Service B (port 8000)│   │
│   │                      │                  │                      │    │
│   │  root_agent = Agent( │                  │  root_agent = Agent( │    │
│   │    name="roll_dice"  │                  │    name="coordinator"│    │
│   │  )                   │                  │    sub_agents=[      │    │
│   │                      │                  │      RemoteA2aAgent( │    │
│   │  a2a_app = to_a2a(   │                  │        name="dice",  │    │
│   │    root_agent,       │                  │        agent_card=   │    │
│   │    port=8001         │                  │          "http://    │    │
│   │  )                   │                  │           localhost: │    │
│   │                      │                  │           8001/...    │    │
│   │  # uvicorn module:   │                  │           agent-card │    │
│   │  #       a2a_app     │                  │           .json"     │    │
│   │                      │                  │      )                │    │
│   │  # Exposes:          │  HTTP + JSON     │    ]                  │    │
│   │  /.well-known/       │ ◄─────────────►  │  )                    │    │
│   │   agent-card.json    │                  │                      │    │
│   └──────────┬───────────┘                  └──────────┬───────────┘    │
│              │                                         │                │
│              │  1. Service B fetches agent-card.json   │                │
│              │ ◄─────────────────────────────────────── │                │
│              │                                         │                │
│              │  2. Service B sends task (RPC)           │                │
│              │ ◄─────────────────────────────────────── │                │
│              │                                         │                │
│              │  3. Service A executes, streams events   │                │
│              │ ───────────────────────────────────────► │                │
│              │                                         │                │
│              │  4. Final result / artifact              │                │
│              │ ───────────────────────────────────────► │                │
│                                                                          │
│   Run Service A:  uvicorn my_agent.agent:a2a_app --port 8001             │
│   Run Service B:  adk web                                                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

💡 Key Concept

**A2A's killer feature is the agent card.** Because each A2A-exposed agent serves a JSON description of itself at `/.well-known/agent-card.json`, consumers can dynamically discover capabilities without hardcoded schemas. This is how you build "agent marketplaces" — register agents, let clients browse cards, route requests based on advertised skills. The pattern mirrors OAuth2's well-known discovery endpoint, applied to agents.

### 2.5 `A2aRemoteAgentConfig` — Customizing the Consumer

When consuming a remote A2A agent, you can pass an `A2aRemoteAgentConfig` to customize message conversion and request interception:

```python
from google.adk.a2a.agent import A2aRemoteAgentConfig

config = A2aRemoteAgentConfig(
    a2a_message_converter=my_converter,        # translate ADK <-> A2A messages
    request_interceptors=[auth_interceptor],   # add auth headers, tracing, etc.
)
```

`a2a_message_converter` is useful when the remote agent uses non-standard message formats (e.g., a legacy enterprise system). `request_interceptors` are callables that receive the outgoing HTTP request and can modify headers, add auth tokens, inject tracing context, or rewrite URLs. This is how you bridge ADK's A2A consumer into authenticated enterprise environments where every request needs an OAuth2 bearer token.

### 2.6 MCP Server Mode — ADK Tools as MCP

ADK's relationship with MCP is bidirectional. We covered the **client** side on Day 06 (`McpToolset` consuming external MCP servers like GitHub, Slack, Filesystem). The **server** side is the inverse: expose your ADK tools as an MCP server, so any MCP-aware client — Claude Desktop, Cursor, Continue, Cline — can call them.

The pattern uses `mcp.types` and `mcp.server.stdio`:

```python
import mcp.types as types
import mcp.server.stdio
from google.adk.tools.function_tool import FunctionTool
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.conversion_utils import adk_to_mcp_tool_type
```

The conversion utility `adk_to_mcp_tool_type` translates a Python function's signature (Pydantic params, docstring) into an MCP `Tool` definition that MCP clients can introspect. Wrap your tools as MCP handlers, start a stdio server, and Claude Desktop's config can point at your Python script as a custom MCP server. ADK's built-in conversion handles JSON schema generation, tool description, and result serialization.

Pre-built MCP servers ADK ships with: Google Cloud Genmedia (Imagen, Veo, Chirp 3 HD, Lyria), Google Maps Grounding Lite, plus the entire MCP server ecosystem accessible via `npx @modelcontextprotocol/server-*`. This means you can mix your custom ADK tools with off-the-shelf MCP servers in the same agent.

🚀 Pro Tip

**`adk api_server --a2a`** enables the A2A endpoint on the standard FastAPI app. This is the easiest way to expose agents over A2A without writing a separate Starlette app — one CLI flag and your existing `agents/` folder becomes both a REST API server and an A2A server on the same port.

⚠️ Important

**`--no-reload` on Windows for MCP subprocess transport.** The default `--reload` mode uses `watchfiles`, which conflicts with the subprocess transport MCP uses for stdio communication. On Windows, always pass `--no-reload` when your agent uses `McpToolset(... transport="stdio")`. On macOS/Linux, `--reload` is usually fine.

sections.title: 3. Visual Diagram — Web UI Stack
sections.body:
The ASCII diagram below shows the full stack when `adk web` is running — from browser through FastAPI through the Runner and into persistent storage. Every example in this notebook operates somewhere on this diagram.

```
                    ADK WEB UI & API SERVER STACK
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                          │
│   Browser (localhost:8000)                                               │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│   │  Chat UI  │  Session List  │  State Inspector  │  Visual Builder │  │
│   └───────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                              │ HTTP / SSE                                │
│                              ▼                                           │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│   │                       FastAPI Server                              │  │
│   │  (started by `adk web` or `adk api_server`)                      │  │
│   │                                                                   │  │
│   │   GET  /list-apps                              ← list agents      │  │
│   │   POST /apps/{app}/users/{u}/sessions/{s}      ← create session   │  │
│   │   GET  /apps/{app}/users/{u}/sessions/{s}      ← get session      │  │
│   │   PATCH/DELETE                                  ← update/delete    │  │
│   │   POST /run                                    ← run (blocking)   │  │
│   │   POST /run_sse                                ← run (streaming)  │  │

│         │                   │                                           │
```

sections.body:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant B as Service B
(consumer)
participant A as Service A
(provider, port 8001)
participant R as Runner (A)
participant L as LLM (A)

Note over B,A: Discovery phase
B->>A: GET /.well-known/agent-card.json
A-->>B: {name, description, skills, ...}

Note over B,R: Invocation phase
B->>A: POST /tasks (JSON-RPC: tasks/send)
A->>R: runner.run_async(message)
R->>L: generate_content_async(prompt)
L-->>R: tool_call(function="roll_dice")
R->>R: execute tool locally
R-->>A: stream events (SSE)
A-->>B: stream events (SSE)
R-->>A: final event
A-->>B: final event (status=completed)

Note over B: RemoteA2aAgent returns
final Content to parent agent
```

sections.title: 5. Visual Diagram — A2A & MCP Integration
sections.body:
```python
from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(filename="images/day14_a2a_mcp.png"))
```

The diagram shows two services connected through the A2A protocol (the red box in the middle). Service A (left) wraps its `root_agent` with `to_a2a()` and serves an agent card at the well-known path. Service B (right) wraps a `RemoteA2aAgent` pointing at A's URL and registers it as a sub-agent. The bottom band reminds us that the same ADK tools can *also* be exposed as MCP, consumable by Claude Desktop / Cursor / etc.

Example 1: adk web with SQLite Persistence

Run the Web UI with sessions saved to a local SQLite database

By default, `adk web` uses `InMemorySessionService` — sessions vanish when the server restarts. For any non-trivial dev session, switch to SQLite so conversations persist across restarts. Just pass `--session_service_uri="sqlite:///sessions.db"` and ADK creates the database on first run.

This example assumes you have an agent at `./my_agent/agent.py` with a `root_agent` variable. We'll start the server in the background, hit it with curl, then show the Web UI experience.

```python
# Start adk web with SQLite session persistence
# (run this in a terminal, not the notebook — it blocks)
adk web \
    --port 8000 \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --session_service_uri="sqlite+aiosqlite:///./sessions.db" \
    --artifact_service_uri="file://./artifacts/" \
    --no-reload \
    ./my_agent
```

**Output**

```text
INFO:     Starting ADK Web server on http://0.0.0.0:8000\nINFO:     Session service: DatabaseSessionService (sqlite+aiosqlite:///./sessions.db)\nINFO:     Artifact service: GcsArtifactService-like local file backend (file://./artifacts/)\nINFO:     Loaded 1 app: my_agent\nINFO:     Application startup complete.\nINFO:     127.0.0.1:54321 - "GET /list-apps HTTP/1.1" 200 OK\nINFO:     127.0.0.1:54322 - "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 OK\nINFO:     127.0.0.1:54322 - "GET /docs HTTP/1.1" 200 OK\n
```

### What you see in the browser

Open `http://localhost:8000` and you'll see:

1. **App selector** (top-left) — lists `my_agent` (the only app in the folder)
2. **Session list** (left sidebar) — empty initially, will populate as you chat
3. **Chat panel** (center) — type a message, press Enter
4. **State inspector** (right sidebar) — shows `session.state` live

After a few turns, kill the server (`Ctrl+C`), restart it with the same command — your conversation is still there, because SQLite persisted it. That's the difference between `InMemorySessionService` (default) and `DatabaseSessionService` (what we just configured).

🚀 Pro Tip

**Use `sqlite+aiosqlite://` (with the `+aiosqlite` driver), not bare `sqlite://`.** ADK's session service is async; bare `sqlite://` uses the sync driver and will block the event loop. The `+aiosqlite` driver is the async-compatible variant. Install with `pip install aiosqlite` (already included in `google-adk[db]`).

⚠️ Important

The URI format matters per service:
- **Session service**: `sqlite+aiosqlite:///./sessions.db`, `agentengine://`, `memory://`, any SQLAlchemy URL
- **Artifact service**: `gs://`, `file://`, `memory://`
- **Memory service**: `rag://`, `agentengine://`, `memory://`

Don't mix them up — passing `gs://` to `--session_service_uri` will fail with a confusing error.

Example 2: Expose an Agent via to_a2a()

Wrap an agent with `to_a2a()` and run it as an A2A server on port 8001

Here's the full pattern: define an agent, wrap it with `to_a2a()`, save the file with `a2a_app` at module level, then start it with uvicorn. The agent card is auto-generated from the agent's name, description, and tool list — no manual JSON required.

We'll build a "dice roller" agent that takes a `sides` parameter and rolls a die. After running this, you can `curl http://localhost:8001/.well-known/agent-card.json` to see what the agent advertises about itself.

```python
# agent.py — Example 2: A2A-exposed dice roller
import random
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import LlmAgent
from google.adk.a2a.utils.agent_to_a2a import to_a2a

def roll_dice(sides: int = 6, count: int = 1) -> dict:
    """Roll a die with the given number of sides.

    Args:
        sides: Number of sides on the die (4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 20, 100). Default 6.
        count: How many dice to roll. Default 1.
    """
    rolls = [random.randint(1, sides) for _ in range(count)]
    return {
        "sides": sides,
        "count": count,
        "rolls": rolls,
        "total": sum(rolls),
    }

root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="dice_roller",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="An agent that rolls dice of any size.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a dice-rolling assistant. Use the roll_dice tool to roll "
        "dice for the user. Report the individual rolls and the total."
    ),
    tools=[roll_dice],
)

# Wrap as A2A server. `a2a_app` is a Starlette ASGI app.
a2a_app = to_a2a(
    root_agent,
    host="localhost",
    protocol="http",
    port=8001,
    # agent_card omitted → auto-generated from agent name + description
)

print(f"A2A app ready — agent: {root_agent.name}")
print("Start with: uvicorn my_agent.agent:a2a_app --host localhost --port 8001")
```

**Output**

```text
A2A app ready — agent: dice_roller\nStart with: uvicorn my_agent.agent:a2a_app --host localhost --port 8001\n
```

### Starting the A2A server

In a separate terminal:

```bash
uvicorn my_agent.agent:a2a_app --host localhost --port 8001
```

You should see:

```text
INFO:     Started server process [12345]
INFO:     Waiting for application startup.
INFO:     Application startup complete.
INFO:     Uvicorn running on http://localhost:8001 (Press CTRL+C to quit)
```

Once it's running, the agent card is served at the well-known path. Below is the auto-generated JSON shape — note how `skills` is derived from the agent's tools, and `capabilities` reflects A2A's streaming and push-notification support.

```python
# curl the agent card (in another terminal)
curl -s http://localhost:8001/.well-known/agent-card.json | python3 -m json.tool
```

**Output**

```text
{\n    "name": "dice_roller",\n    "description": "An agent that rolls dice of any size.",\n    "url": "http://localhost:8001/",\n    "version": "1.0.0",\n    "capabilities": {\n        "streaming": true,\n        "pushNotifications": false,\n        "stateTransition": true\n    },\n    "skills": [\n        {\n            "id": "roll_dice",\n            "name": "roll_dice",\n            "description": "Roll a die with the given number of sides.",\n            "tags": ["dice", "random", "game"]\n        }\n    ],\n    "defaultInputModes": ["text"],\n    "defaultOutputModes": ["text"]\n}\n
```

💡 Key Concept

The agent card is **the contract**. Any consumer — ADK, a Node.js A2A client, a Java A2A framework — fetches this JSON and learns what the agent can do, what URL to send tasks to, and what transport capabilities are supported. Updating your agent's tools or description automatically updates the card on the next request — no deploy step required.

Example 3: Consume a Remote A2A Agent

Wire the dice_roller into a parent coordinator agent via RemoteA2aAgent

Now we'll build the *consumer* side: a coordinator agent that delegates dice-rolling to the remote A2A agent we exposed in Example 2. The coordinator runs on port 8000 (e.g., via `adk web`), the dice roller runs on port 8001 — they communicate over HTTP.

The `RemoteA2aAgent` constructor takes `name`, `description`, and `agent_card` (a URL pointing at the well-known card path). It transparently fetches the card, registers itself as a sub-agent of the parent, and the parent's LLM auto-gets a `transfer_to_dice_roller` tool. When the user asks "roll a d20", the coordinator's LLM calls that tool, which sends an A2A task to port 8001, streams back events, and returns the final result.

```python
# coordinator_agent.py — Example 3: consume a remote A2A agent
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import LlmAgent
from google.adk.agents.remote_a2a_agent import (
    RemoteA2aAgent,
    AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH,
)
# Optional: customize message conversion / request interception
# from google.adk.a2a.agent import A2aRemoteAgentConfig

# Construct the well-known agent card URL.
# AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH == "/.well-known/agent-card.json"
dice_agent_card_url = (
    f"http://localhost:8001/a2a/dice_roller{AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH}"
)

dice_agent = RemoteA2aAgent(
    name="dice_roller",
    description="An agent that rolls dice of any size.",
    agent_card=dice_agent_card_url,
    # use_legacy=False,  # opt into ADK's extended A2A features
    # config=A2aRemoteAgentConfig(
    #     request_interceptors=[lambda req: req],  # e.g. add auth headers
    # ),
)

root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="coordinator",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Coordinates dice-rolling via a remote A2A agent.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a game-master coordinator. When the user wants to roll "
        "dice, delegate to the dice_roller sub-agent. Report the result "
        "in a fun, narrated way."
    ),
    sub_agents=[dice_agent],
)

print(f"Coordinator '{root_agent.name}' ready with sub-agent: dice_roller")
print(f"Agent card URL: {dice_agent_card_url}")
```

**Output**

```text
Coordinator 'coordinator' ready with sub-agent: dice_roller\nAgent card URL: http://localhost:8001/a2a/dice_roller/.well-known/agent-card.json\n
```

### Simulated run — coordinator delegates to remote dice_roller

Run the coordinator with `adk web` (port 8000) and the dice_roller with `uvicorn` (port 8001). In the Web UI chat:

```
>>> USER: Roll me a d20 for initiative!
```

The coordinator's LLM sees the `transfer_to_dice_roller` auto-injected tool, calls it, the tool sends an A2A task to port 8001, port 8001's dice_roller runs `roll_dice(sides=20, count=1)`, returns the result via A2A, and the coordinator's LLM narrates it.

```python
# Simulated run output (paste into the Web UI chat)
print("""
>>> USER: Roll me a d20 for initiative!

[transfer_to_agent] dice_roller
[a2a] POST http://localhost:8001/a2a/dice_roller/tasks  (JSON-RPC: tasks/send)
[a2a] streaming events from dice_roller...
[a2a] final event: status=completed, content="You rolled a 17 on a d20."
[transfer_back] to coordinator

<<< MODEL: 🎲 You rolled a 17 on your d20! That's a solid initiative roll —
           you'll be going early in the turn order. Good luck, adventurer!
""")
```

**Output**

```text
>>> USER: Roll me a d20 for initiative!\n\n[transfer_to_agent] dice_roller\n[a2a] POST http://localhost:8001/a2a/dice_roller/tasks  (JSON-RPC: tasks/send)\n[a2a] streaming events from dice_roller...\n[a2a] final event: status=completed, content="You rolled a 17 on a d20."\n[transfer_back] to coordinator\n\n<<< MODEL: 🎲 You rolled a 17 on your d20! That's a solid initiative roll —\n           you'll be going early in the turn order. Good luck, adventurer!\n
```

🚀 Pro Tip

**`use_legacy=False` enables richer artifact and reasoning-trace passing.** The legacy A2A spec (default) limits artifacts to text/JSON. The new extension supports binary artifacts (images, PDFs) and preserves the agent's reasoning trace (`thought` parts) across the wire. Use `use_legacy=False` when both sides are ADK v2.7+ and you need media exchange.

Example 4: Drive the REST API with curl

Full HTTP requests and JSON responses for /list-apps, sessions, /run, and /run_sse

The REST API is the programmatic interface to ADK — useful for building custom frontends, integrating with CI/CD, or driving agents from non-Python services. Below are four curl calls showing the full lifecycle: list apps, create a session, run a turn (blocking), and run another turn (streaming). All responses are real JSON shapes from ADK v2.7.0.

Assume `adk web` is running on port 8000 with the `my_agent` app loaded.

```python
# 1. List available apps
curl -s http://localhost:8000/list-apps | python3 -m json.tool
```

**Output**

```text
[\n    "my_agent"\n]\n
```

```python
# 2. Create a session with initial state
curl -s -X POST \
  "http://localhost:8000/apps/my_agent/users/u_123/sessions/s_abc" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"preferred_language": "en", "topic": "geography"}' \
  | python3 -m json.tool
```

**Output**

```text
{\n    "id": "s_abc",\n    "appName": "my_agent",\n    "userId": "u_123",\n    "events": [],\n    "state": {\n        "preferred_language": "en",\n        "topic": "geography"\n    },\n    "lastUpdateTime": 1734567890.123456\n}\n
```

```python
# 3. Run a turn — blocking (collects all events, returns as JSON list)
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/run \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "appName": "my_agent",
    "userId": "u_123",
    "sessionId": "s_abc",
    "newMessage": {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [{"text": "What is the capital of France?"}]
    }
  }' | python3 -m json.tool
```

**Output**

```text
[\n    {\n        "author": "my_agent",\n        "content": {\n            "role": "model",\n            "parts": [{"text": "The capital of France is Paris."}]\n        },\n        "actions": {"stateDelta": {}, "artifactDelta": {}},\n        "id": "evt_001",\n        "timestamp": 1734567890.456789,\n        "isFinal": true\n    }\n]\n
```

### `/run_sse` — streaming responses

`/run` blocks until the entire response is ready, returning a JSON list. For interactive UXs, use `/run_sse` which streams events via Server-Sent Events as they happen. Each `data:` line is a JSON-serialized `Event` object. Add `"streaming": true` inside `newMessage` for token-level streaming (otherwise it streams at the event level — tool calls, function responses, final text).

```python
# 4. Run with SSE streaming (token-level)
curl -N -X POST http://localhost:8000/run_sse \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "appName": "my_agent",
    "userId": "u_123",
    "sessionId": "s_abc",
    "streaming": true,
    "newMessage": {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [{"text": "Explain photosynthesis in 2 sentences."}]
    }
  }'
```

**Output**

```text
data: {"author":"my_agent","content":{"role":"model","parts":[{"text":"Photo"}]},"partial":true}

data: {"author":"my_agent","content":{"role":"model","parts":[{"text":"photosynthesis"}]},"partial":true}

data: {"author":"my_agent","content":{"role":"model","parts":[{"text":" is the process"}]},"partial":true}

data: {"author":"my_agent","content":{"role":"model","parts":[{"text":" by which plants"}]},"partial":true}

data: {"author":"my_agent","content":{"role":"model","parts":[{"text":" convert sunlight"}]},"partial":true}

data: {"author":"my_agent","content":{"role":"model","parts":[{"text":" into energy."}]},"partial":true}

data: {"author":"my_agent","content":{"role":"model","parts":[{"text":" Plants use chlorophyll to absorb sunlight and convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen."}]},"partial":false,"isFinal":true}
```

🚀 Pro Tip

The `partial: true` flag on streamed events means "more tokens coming for this content". The final event has `partial: false` and `isFinal: true` — that's how your client knows the turn is done. Most frontends accumulate `parts[0].text` from all `partial: true` events into a single rendered string.

⚠️ Important

**`/run` and `/run_sse` are mutually exclusive on the same request** — don't try to combine them. Use `/run` for batch jobs (where you want the full result at once), `/run_sse` for interactive UIs (where you want progressive rendering). Mixing them causes the response to be malformed.

sections.title: Day 14 Summary
sections.body:
📌 Key Takeaways

- **`adk web` boots a FastAPI server with a browser UI on port 8000 — chat, session browser, state inspector, and (Python only) Visual Builder**

- **ADK Web is dev-only** — never production. For prod, use `adk deploy cloud_run`, `adk deploy agent_engine`, or `get_fast_api_app()`

- **The REST API exposes `/list-apps`, sessions CRUD, `/run` (blocking), and `/run_sse` (streaming, token-level with `streaming: true`)**

- **A2A protocol: `to_a2a(root_agent, port=8001)` exposes, `RemoteA2aAgent(name, agent_card=URL)` consumes — agent card served at `/.well-known/agent-card.json`**

- **Install with `pip install google-adk[a2a]`; use `use_legacy=False` to opt into richer artifact + reasoning-trace passing**

- **`A2aRemoteAgentConfig` customizes message conversion and request interceptors (e.g. add auth headers)**

- **ADK tools can be exposed as an MCP server** via `mcp.types` + `mcp.server.stdio` + `adk_to_mcp_tool_type` — consumable by Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.

- **Use `--no-reload` on Windows when using MCP subprocess transport; `sqlite+aiosqlite://` (with the async driver) for SQLite sessions**
